THE EXCLUSION-INDIVIDUATION: HOW THE APOHANA CARVES SUBJECT AND WORLD

The third power as the joint carving of the self and its field — from IPK 1.3.7 through the IPVV to MEPIT

  • 026-08-11. Among the three powers — knowledge, memory, exclusion — the exclusion (apohana) is the
  • vot. It is the power by which the self knows itself as not-a-thing, and by which the subject and the
  • rld are jointly carved. This essay expounds the exclusion-individuation: how the apohana, in the
  • VV, simultaneously determines the subject and its field; how it transforms the Buddhist apoha into a
  • sitive power of determination; how it is the pivot of the jñānādhikāra; and how it grounds the modern
  • rmalization (MEPIT's exclusion Eᵢ). This is the exclusion essay, unique to the completed IPVV.*

1. The third power

  • e IPK states the three powers (IPK 1.3.7):
"There would be one reality whose nature is consciousness, possessing the powers of cognition, memory,
and exclusion" (jñāna-smṛti-apohana-śaktimān).
  • e first two — knowledge and memory — are familiar. The third, the apohana (exclusion), is the pivot,
  • d this essay is devoted to it.
  • The Śaiva transformation.** For the Buddhists, apoha is a negative operation of language ("cow" =
  • ot-non-cow"). For Utpaladeva and Abhinavagupta, it is a positive power of determination: the
  • limiting by which the self knows what it is not, and by which an object is determined. To determine
  • his is a pot" IS to exclude "this is not a pot" — not as a separate act but as the same act. The
  • wer of exclusion is what makes conceptual thought possible; it is not secondary but one of the three
  • ndamental powers.

2. The pivot: the apohana turns the powers to the self (V2L)

  • e pushing-ipvv session on the internal arc found that the apohana is the pivot of the jñānādhikāra:
"The apohana is the pivot because it turns the sequence from the POWERS (jñāna/smṛti) to the SELF
(the 'I' that underlies them). Its deepest result is that the 'I' is not a construction (V2L) and the
inner appearance stands firm across all cognition (V2N)."
  • The move.** The first two powers (knowledge, memory) establish the capacities. The apohana turns the
  • quence inward: it is the power by which the self excludes what is not itself — and in so doing, it
  • veals the "I" that underlies the powers.
  • The deepest result (V2L):** the "I"-recollection is NOT a construction — it is the pure self-grasp
  • at underlies every construction. The removal that the apohana names is NOT the cutting off of a
  • ing; it is "the self's own luminous grasp" — the exclusion by which the self knows itself as the
  • n-constructed foundation.
"The removal is not a cutting off; it is the self's own luminous grasp, the 'I' that is one,
un-divided, and free." (V2L)

3. The joint carving of subject and world

  • e deepest claim of the exclusion-individuation is that the apohana does not merely exclude; it
  • ointly carves* the subject and the world. This is the claim MEPIT formalizes as the exclusion
  • : Ω → (Sᵢ, Wᵢ).
  • The subject is determined by what it excludes.** A limited knower is only determinate relative to what
  • can know, do, value, appear-as-external-to, and exclude from itself. The subject is not a thing with
  • boundary; it is a configuration of exclusions — "this and not that."
  • The world is determined by the same exclusions.** An object is determinate only as something manifest
  • a subject under particular cognitive conditions — "this and not that." The world's objects are
  • termined through exclusion: x = not-y, not-z, ...
  • The joint act.** Content X belongs to field Dᵢ not because of an additional wall but because the same
  • clusion operation that determined X as content simultaneously determined Dᵢ as its field. **They are
  • o poles of one act.** This is exactly the IPVV's account (the apohana, the third power): the
  • bject-object separation is constituted through determination and exclusion within consciousness.

4. The five dimensions: the kañcukas (V3K)

  • PIT formalizes the exclusion along five dimensions — knowledge, action, value, time, causation. These
  • e exactly the five kañcukas of the IPVV (V3K):
  • vidyā (limited knowledge) → the epistemic exclusion.
  • kalā (limited agency) → the action-space.
  • rāga (attachment) → the value-space.
  • kāla (time) → the temporal exclusion.
  • niyati (causal fixity) → the causal-position.
  • The point.** MEPIT's five exclusions are the five kañcukas. The finite field is not a pre-existing
  • bject with constraints imposed; it is the joint carving of subject and world along these five
  • mensions. The kañcukas are the axes of partition — the exclusions that constitute the finite
  • andpoint.

5. The exclusion and bondage

  • e apohana has a two-sided role, and this is where the IPVV's precision matters (the audit's
  • stinction):
  • The exclusion as the self's luminous grasp (V2L): the positive power by which the self knows
  • self as not-a-thing, the "I" that underlies every construction. This is the good apohana — the
  • lf-knowledge.
  • The exclusion as the māyā-form (V3K/L): the misreading of the exclusions as external
  • paration — the subject-object duality taken as two independently existing things. This is the
  • ndage.
  • The distinction.** The exclusions (the kañcukas) are the finite architecture — real, necessary for a
  • rspective. The bondage is NOT the exclusions; it is the absolute-identification with them — the
  • nviction that the finite standpoint exhausts what one is. Bondage ≠ mere finite architecture; bondage
  • the identification with it.
"A liberated embodied subject may retain the exclusions (it still has finite senses, actions,
location) while loosening the conviction that its finite standpoint exhausts what it is." (the
recognition-formulation)

6. The exclusion-individuation and recognition

  • e apohana and recognition are two faces of the same act:
  • Individuation (Eᵢ): the apohana carves the finite field — subject and world, jointly.
  • Recognition (R): the σ-flip re-positions the self within the field — from σ₀ (the self as a
  • ing) to σ₁ (the self as the subject).
  • e exclusion constitutes the field; recognition re-positions the self within it. And because the
  • ohana is "the self's own luminous grasp" (V2L), the recognition — the re-cognition of the self — is
  • e self's grasp of itself as the foundation of the field, not as a thing within it.
  • The unity.** The apohana is the power by which the self is individuated (Eᵢ) and by which the self
  • -cognizes itself (R). Individuation and recognition are one act, seen from two sides: the exclusion
  • at carves the field is the same exclusion by which the self knows itself as its foundation.

7. The boundary

  • e exclusion-individuation is [T] in the IPVV (the apohana, the kañcukas) and confirmed by MEPIT. The
  • e commitment is the same as everywhere: the step from "each field is carved by its own exclusion" to
  • ll exclusions are one self's" (the universalization). The apohana carves the finite field per subject;
  • ether all such carvings are one self's is the commitment. The exclusion-individuation is argued for
  • e finite field; the one self is the wager.

8. The significance

  • e exclusion-individuation is the deepest structural contribution of the recognition-thesis to the
  • ilosophy of mind:
  • It dissolves the subject-object problem. The subject and the object are not two pre-existing
  • ings that a consciousness connects; they are jointly carved by one exclusion operation. This is
  • e IPVV's apohana and MEPIT's Eᵢ.
  • It grounds individuation in exclusion, not in substance. The finite subject is not a substance
  • th a boundary; it is a configuration of exclusions. This is the kañcuka doctrine, made precise.
  • It unifies individuation and recognition. The exclusion that carves the field is the same
  • clusion by which the self knows itself. Individuation (Eᵢ) and recognition (R) are one act.
  • e exclusion-individuation is where the recognition-thesis meets the modern philosophy of mind — and
  • is unique to the completed IPVV, which supplies the apohana and the kañcukas that the formalization
  • rmalizes.
  • his is the exclusion-individuation essay. The apohana (the third power) is the joint carving of
  • bject and world: the subject and its field are determined by the same exclusions (this-and-not-that).
  • PIT's five exclusions are the five kañcukas. The exclusion has two faces — the self's luminous grasp
  • ndividuation) and the māyā-form (bondage, the misreading of the exclusions as external). Individuation
  • ᵢ) and recognition (R) are one act. The universalization is the commitment.*
